extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, scholars, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Academic analysis of how key patent-validity doctrines (subject-matter eligibility/Alice, anticipation/§102, written description/§112, enablement) implicate legal-vs-factual questions and the procedural consequences (pleadings, jury, standard of review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step patent-eligibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court’s two-step test: first ask whether a claim is 'directed to' an ineligible concept (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon); second, if so, ask whether, setting aside the ineligible principle, the patent contains 'additional elements' that 'transform' the claim into a 'patent-eligible application' of the underlying principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing that the patent recites 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional activity' is one way to show that the patent does not qualify as an application of the underlying, ineligible principle. (Cites: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int’l; Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Alice step two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a patent involves well-understood, routine, or conventional activity is treated by the Federal Circuit as a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That factual determination can depend on evidence such as trial testimony about the state of the art and may therefore raise disputes of fact that can require a jury trial (Berkheimer v. HP). It is used to assess whether claimed 'additional elements' provide an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim specificity versus prior-art comparison in Alice step two
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Federal Circuit decisions emphasize the specificity of the claims themselves (their concrete, discrete implementation) rather than how the claimed invention compares to previously known technology when resolving step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have sometimes refused to consider evidence of novelty or nonobviousness when deciding step two, instead pinning rulings on claim breadth or specific claim limitations (e.g., Bascom, Two-Way Media, Affinity Labs). This approach resembles claim construction and treats the issue more as a legal determination about claim scope than a fact-driven inquiry into the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of what a claim is 'directed to' (Alice step one)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step one asks whether a patent claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon; determining what a claim is 'directed to' can look like the legal task of claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has instructed that comparing the claimed invention to prior precedent is a key method for deciding the question (e.g., Enfish). Some district courts treat Alice Step One as a 'purely legal question' and may decide it based solely on intrinsic evidence; other courts have relied on extrinsic sources (textbooks, treatises) indicating a more fact-driven analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intrinsic versus extrinsic evidence in Alice step one
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts differ on whether to decide step one based only on intrinsic evidence (the patent and prosecution history) or to consider extrinsic evidence about the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CardioNet holds Alice step one presents a legal question answerable from intrinsic evidence; other cases (and Supreme Court opinions) have relied on extrinsic materials (textbooks, treatises, expert evidence) to characterize claimed concepts as abstract or longstanding practices (Bilski, Alice, Intell. Ventures v. Cap. One).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Fundamental economic practice' standard invites factual inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have written that a patent recites an abstract idea when it claims 'a fundamental economic practice long prevalent in our system of commerce,' a standard that invites inquiry into historical/practical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this standard asks whether a practice is 'longstanding,' courts and judges have looked to extrinsic evidence and factual determinations (see Solutran; CardioNet dissent noting relevance of extrinsic evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena eligibility involves factual questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether a claim involves a law of nature or a natural phenomenon requires determining whether the claimed subject matter exists in the world without human intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad illustrates invalidation when claimed DNA sequences 'existed in nature before' discovery; courts have relied on witness testimony and extrinsic evidence to determine whether claimed subject matter is natural (e.g., Myriad; American Axle; BRCA litigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/Jury implications when eligibility depends on factual disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: If resolving eligibility requires consideration of evidence and factual disputes, that may require submission to a jury and affects when and how eligibility can be resolved (pleadings, motions, trial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show variation: eligibility has been decided on JMOL/post-trial motion based on trial evidence, been reserved for juries, or decided as a matter of law on the pleadings. The uncertainty extends to whether pleadings must meet Twombly/Iqbal plausibility when alleging facts relevant to eligibility and whether juries may determine eligibility or only subsidiary factual issues (examples: Chamberlain, iLife, PPS Data, Genetic Veterinary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate question of patent validity is legal, but subsidiary issues may be factual
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Supreme Court has said patent validity is ultimately a question of law, many important doctrines involve subsidiary factual determinations that can affect the ultimate legal conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit treats several doctrines (anticipation, written description, utility) as presenting factual questions in practice, creating tension with Supreme Court pronouncements and producing uncertainty about procedure and standard of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (§102) — novelty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is invalid for anticipation if the exact same invention was previously disclosed; §102 distinguishes prior inventions by others and the patentee’s own prior disclosure (statutory bar), and the AIA revised these provisions for applications filed on/after March 16, 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA: §102(a) (prior invention by others) and §102(b) (statutory bar; >1 year prior public use/sale/printed publication). AIA §102(a)(1)–(2) now treats prior patents, printed publications, public use, on sale, or otherwise publicly available before filing date (and certain published applications) as prior art, while preserving a one-year grace period for the inventor's own disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation as a question of fact (and element-by-element comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has repeatedly described anticipation as a question of fact — often because anticipation requires finding each element of the claimed invention in a single prior art reference (an element-by-element factual comparison).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate opinions state anticipation is a factual question (Brown v. 3M; In re Gleave; Microsoft v. Biscotti), but many subsidiary issues (e.g., whether a reference is a 'printed publication') are treated as legal questions. The element-by-element comparison is analogous to the fact question of infringement, which juries typically decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication and incorporation-by-reference determinations (as legal questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a prior reference qualifies as a 'printed publication' or incorporates extraneous material by reference is treated as a question of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts resolve these threshold issues as legal determinations (e.g., Advanced Display Sys. v. Kent State Univ.; GoPro v. Contour). These legal gatekeeping decisions determine whether a reference may be used for the factual anticipation comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception and reduction-to-practice determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about when an invention was conceived and reduced to practice (relevant under pre-AIA §102) are characterized as questions of law subject to de novo review, though they rest on underlying factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybritech treated conception/reduction-to-practice as legal questions; more recent cases (e.g., Barry v. Medtronic) have called reduction to practice a mixed question of law and fact and applied deferential review to jury findings when supported by substantial evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use/on-sale and experimental-use analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an invention was in public use or on sale (relevant to §102 pre- and post-AIA) and whether a use was experimental (and thus not invalidating) involve factual inquiries but are treated as law based on the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has described these questions as legal determinations grounded in fact (Netscape v. Konrad; Lough v. Brunswick). Courts evaluate the totality of circumstances to determine experimental use or public use status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (§112) — possession and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description polices claim breadth by ensuring the inventor actually invented what the patent claims: (1) it prevents adding claims not supported by the original disclosure; (2) it invalidates patents when the specification indicates the inventor was not in possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: Gentry Gallery (original application described an 'essential element' limiting claimed subject matter), Eli Lilly (specification disclosed rat insulin sequence but claimed human insulin). The Federal Circuit (Ariad en banc) treats written description as a question of fact; the inquiry 'depends on the nature of the invention and the amount of knowledge imparted to those skilled in the art' and typically involves documentary comparison, expert testimony, and a person-of-ordinary-skill perspective—much like claim construction. Written-description issues often reach juries and are reviewed deferentially on appeal, in contrast to de novo review of claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (§112) (relation to written description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is the companion requirement in §112 that ensures the specification teaches how to make and use the claimed invention (i.e., enables a person of ordinary skill in the art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is described as written description’s 'close cousin'—both derive from §112 and overlap in function—though the page only begins the enablement discussion here. Enablement inquiries likewise involve technical documentary evidence and may raise mixed law-fact issues.
